Why a cup doesn't have one weight

Cups measure how much space something takes up. Grams measure how heavy it is. A cup of honey and a cup of cocoa powder take up the same space, but the honey weighs four times as much, so a converter has to know the ingredient before it can give an answer. Any site that gives one number for every ingredient is really telling you the weight of water.

Even for a single ingredient, the way you fill the cup matters. Flour scooped from the bag can weigh 20% more than flour spooned in and leveled. That's the main reason recipes turn out differently from kitchen to kitchen, and why weighing is worth the switch if you bake often.

Questions

How many grams are in a cup?

It depends on the ingredient, because a cup measures volume and grams measure weight. A US cup of water weighs about 237 g, all-purpose flour 120 g, granulated sugar 200 g and butter 227 g. Pick the ingredient in the converter to get the right number.

How do I convert grams to cups?

Choose grams as the unit, type the weight, and pick the ingredient. The converter divides by that ingredient’s weight per cup and rounds to the nearest kitchen fraction, like ⅓ or ¾ cup.

Is this a US cup or a metric cup?

US cups, which hold 236.6 ml. Metric cups, used in Australia, New Zealand and many Canadian and UK recipes, hold 250 ml, about 6% more. If your recipe uses metric cups, multiply the grams here by 1.06.

Why do other sites give a different number for flour?

Because they measure differently. Spooned and leveled, a cup of all-purpose flour is about 120 g. Scooped straight from the bag it packs down to 135–145 g. This site uses the spoon-and-level weights most recipe writers expect, and each ingredient page lists its source.
